# Psalm 78:49–72: research notes

**About these notes:** I didn't have enough lookups to cover everything. Enduring Word's page cut off before verse 49, so I've only used its section summaries. Two pages would not load at all: the full Pulpit Commentary page on StudyLight and Spurgeon's Treasury of David on Blue Letter Bible. Verses 52–55 and 63–64 are thin or missing. I found nothing from the Lutheran, Pentecostal, Catholic-commentary, Orthodox or Bible Odyssey sites. Unless I say otherwise, the older commentators come from Bible Hub and StudyLight compilation pages.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 49 ("destroying angels")**
- **Most commentators say these angels aren't wicked in themselves.** They're called "evil" because they brought evil, meaning disaster, on Egypt. Gill, Barnes and Coffman all say this. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/78-49.html
- **Barnes and the Cambridge Bible tie this to the "destroyer" who killed the firstborn** (Exodus 12:23). Cambridge calls them destroying angels sent by God to carry out punishment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-49.htm
- **Clarke** counts this as the first mention of "evil angels" and says we can't tell what they were. He notes that some link them to the angel who killed the firstborn, but points out that verse 51 mentions that separately. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/78-49.html
- **Barnes:** the pile-up of anger words (fury, wrath, indignation, trouble) is there because this was the last and worst plague. https://www.studylight.org/bible/heb/hmd/psalms/78-49.html
- **Matthew Henry:** good angels become "evil angels" to sinners. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/78-49.html
- **Spurgeon:** God saved his sharpest arrow for last. The same angels who serve God's people carry out judgment on his enemies. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps078.cfm
- **Gill and Poole mention a minority view** that the "messengers of evil" were Moses and Aaron, who kept bringing Pharaoh bad news. Gill also notes that some think demons were sent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-49.htm

**vv. 50–51**
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB):** "cleared a path" (KJV "made a way") means God removed every obstacle and gave his anger full scope. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_078.cfm
- **Cambridge:** verses 49–51 are the climax of the plagues, the death of the firstborn. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-49.htm

**vv. 52–55**
- **Guzik's summary of verses 40–55:** each plague showed God was greater than Egypt's gods. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/
- I found no verse-level notes on the sheep imagery, the sea, or the settling of the land.

**vv. 56–58**
- **Guzik:** Israel's typical sin changed from complaining in the wilderness to idolatry in Canaan. He calls it a paradox: God used Israel to judge idol-worshippers, and Israel then became idol-worshippers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/
- **Constable:** after Joshua died, the people tested God by not driving out the Canaanites, then turned to false gods. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/78-60.html
- **Coffman:** Israel was copying the very behaviour that got the seven Canaanite nations replaced. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/78-60.html

**v. 59**
- **Coffman:** "On hearing it" is human language used of God. God already knew everything. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/78-60.html

**v. 60 (Shiloh abandoned)**
- **Ellicott and Benson:** this refers to the defeat by the Philistines and the loss of the ark in 1 Samuel 4. Benson adds that God never returned to Shiloh. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-60.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** God counted as having "forsaken" Shiloh when he let the ark be taken. The tent itself moved later to Nob and then Gibeon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-60.htm
- **Clarke:** God was offended mainly with the priests, who had defiled his worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/78-60.html
- **Gill and Poole:** "among men" shows how far God stooped to live among sinful people. Gill also mentions Lightfoot's unusual reading, "the tent he fixed in Adam" (the town by the Jordan). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-60.htm
- **Spurgeon:** shameless sin at the tent door led to "Ichabod" (the glory has departed). He warns that the gospel can likewise be taken from a church and never restored. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps078.cfm
- **Guzik:** God's glory leaving was not abandonment but a withdrawal of blessing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-78/
- **Bible Hub's own notes:** holy places don't guarantee God's favour; obedience is what matters. They link to Jeremiah 7:12 and to John 1:14, where the Word "tabernacled" among us. https://biblehub.com/psalms/78-60.htm

**v. 61 ("His strength… His splendor")**
- **Keil and Delitzsch:** the ark is called God's strength and glory because it was where he was present and made himself known. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-60.htm
- **Ellicott** links "strength" to Psalm 132:8. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-60.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** letting the ark be captured showed God had given up even the ark as a sign of his presence. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/78-60.html

**v. 62**
- **Matthew Henry:** the people God had chosen became the people of his wrath. Deliberate sins, especially idolatry, make even Israelites offensive to his holiness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/78-60.html

**v. 65 (God waking "as from sleep")**
- **Gill, Barnes and Cambridge:** God only seemed asleep while the ark was captured. He "awoke" when he struck the Philistines and their idol fell before the ark. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-65.htm and https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/jps/psalms/78-65.html
- **The wine picture:** Gill, Clarke and Henry all say it describes a warrior refreshed by a moderate drink, not a drunk man. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/brl/psalms/78-65.html and https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_078.cfm
- **Benson** defends the image by comparing it to Christ coming "like a thief." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-65.htm
- **Coffman:** this is another human-language picture; God had not really been asleep. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/78-65.html

**v. 66**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** this refers to Israel's victories over the Philistines, beginning under Samuel and continuing under Saul and David. "Everlasting shame" means lasting disgrace. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-78.html
- **Matthew Henry** links the shame to the golden tumour models the Philistines sent back with the ark (1 Samuel 6). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_078.cfm

**vv. 67–68**
- **Matthew Henry:** God never sent the ark back to Shiloh in Ephraim. The ruins stood as a monument to his justice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/78-60.html
- **Barnes:** worship moved for good from Ephraim to Judah and Mount Zion. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/jps/psalms/78-60.html
- **A writer quoted by Spurgeon** thinks the whole psalm was prompted by this move from Ephraim to Judah. Ephraim had first held the spiritual advantage because the ark was at Shiloh. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps078.cfm

**v. 69**
- **Matthew Henry:** the sanctuary stood as firm as the earth while it lasted. It wasn't finally destroyed until the gospel temple had been built. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_078.cfm
- **Keil and Delitzsch:** "forever" refers to the place where God reveals himself and his promise to live in Judah, not to the stone building. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-60.htm

**vv. 70–72**
- **Barnes:** "integrity" literally means "perfection of heart." "Skillful hands" is literally "the understanding of his hands" (compare Psalm 144:1). https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/niv/psalms/78-72.html
- **Clarke:** the verse speaks of David's reign as finished. His skill in war led Israel to victory. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/78-72.html
- **On the Bible Hub page (Henry's wording):** David ruled honestly and wisely. The psalm ends with him as the crowning example of God's kindness because he points to Christ, the Good Shepherd. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-72.htm
- **Coffman:** the "forever" kingdom looks past David's line to the risen Christ on his heavenly throne. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/78-65.html

## 2. Differences between Protestant traditions

I found no real disagreement between traditions in what I read. The nearest things:
- **Geneva Bible notes (Reformed), v. 49:** they allow two views. The angels may be named for what they did, or they may have been wicked spirits God allowed to trouble people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-49.htm
- **Geneva Bible notes, v. 65:** because the people were "drunk in their sins," they thought God's patience was asleep. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-65.htm
- **Benson (Methodist), v. 60:** he draws the lesson that only being made new by the Holy Spirit can cure ungodliness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-60.htm
- **Calvin, v. 60:** Shiloh was the one place God had chosen on earth, and he was forced to leave it by the people's constant wickedness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/78-60.html

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- **v. 49:** Pulpit says most modern critics take "wrath, indignation and trouble" to be the "evil angels" themselves. Hengstenberg and Kay think they were real good angels acting as "ministers of woe." https://biblehub.com/psalms/78-49.htm
- **v. 49, NET Bible wording:** "messengers who bring disaster." https://biblehub.com/psalms/78-49.htm
- **v. 65, NET Bible wording:** "a warrior in a drunken rage." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/brl/psalms/78-65.html
- **Shiloh's history:** Keil and Delitzsch say it isn't known when the Shiloh building was destroyed, possibly not until the Assyrian period. They say God's rejection of Shiloh came before its destruction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/78-60.htm
- **Date of the psalm:** Pulpit notes that some critics date it after the Exile. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-78.html

**Catholic (translation only; I found no commentary)**
- **Douay-Rheims:** "evil angels" in v. 49, "surfeited with wine" in v. 65, and "innocence of his heart" in v. 72. https://biblehub.com/psalms/78-49.htm, https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/jps/psalms/78-65.html, https://biblehub.com/psalms/78-72.htm

**Orthodox and popular modern teaching (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace):** nothing found.
